html.body: Date: 2025-03-27 REMARKSUpon entry of the present amendments, claims 30-57 will be pending. Claims 53-57 are withdrawn being directed to non-elected subject-matter.Amendments to the Specification The specification has been amended at page 8 to replace the heading "Description of Drawings" with "Brief Description of Drawings" as suggested by the Office.The specification has also been amended at page 26 to remove the browser-executable code.No new matter has been added by the present amendment.Claim Amendments Without agreeing with any of the present bases of rejection, Applicant has amended claim 30. Support for this amendment can be found throughout the application as filed.No new matter has been added by the present amendments to the claims. Applicant reserves the right to pursue any cancelled subject-matter in this or a continuation application.Claim Objection Claim 30 is objected to because of the recitation of the conjunction "and" at line 9 of claim 30. As Applicant has amended claim 30 to remove the conjunction at line 9, this objection should be withdrawn.35 U.S.C. § 101 Claims 30-52 are rejected for allegedly not being "directed to a judicial exception without significantly more" (Office Action, page 3). Specifically, the Office states at page 10 of the Office Action:The claim limitations do not transform the abstract idea that they recite into patent-eligible subject matter because "the claims simply instruct the practitioner to implement the abstract idea with routine, conventional activity." Applicant respectfully disagrees. Independent claim 30 recites in step (e) "transferring a pre- implantation embryo into the human subject identified as having a receptive endometrial status." Taken as a whole, independent claim 30 does not recite an abstract idea nor a solely "mental" process as independent claim 30 recites in step (e) an additional element that amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception. Therefore, independent claim 30 as a whole is directed to the application of a specific treatment, rather than being "directed to" a judicial exception as it is drawn to patent eligible subject matter. Applicant respectfully submits that in view of the USPTO's Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, and claim 30 as previously presented, the rejection with respect to claim 30 and its dependent claims 31-52 should be reconsidered and withdrawn.35 U.S.C. § 103 1. Claims 30, 32-36, 38-46, and 49-52 are rejected for allegedly being obvious over Diaz- Gimeno et al. (Diaz-Gimeno, Fertility and Sterility 95(1): 50-60 (2011), hereinafter "Diaz- Gimeno I") in view of Almog et al. (Fertility and Sterility 94(6): 2026-2029 (2010); hereinafter "Almog") and Garrido-Gomez et al. (Fertility and Sterility 99(4): 1078-1085 (2013), hereinafter "Garrido-Gomez").In order to establish aprimafacie case of obviousness, the Office must show, that the claimed invention "as a whole" would have been obvious, at the time the application was filed, to a person of ordinary skill in the art based upon the combination of references cited by the Office. Aprimafacie case of obviousness requires (1) all claim limitations to be taught or suggested by the cited references; (2) a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teachings of the prior art references to achieve the claimed invention; and (3) a reasonable expectation of success in making the combination. See, e.g., PAR Pharm., Inc. v. TWIPharm., Inc., 773 F.3d 1186, 1193 (Fed. Cir. 2014). Applicant respectfully submits that the Office's burden has not been carried.Applicant respectfully disagrees that the claims under examination are obvious over the combination of the cited references. There is no suggestion in the combined teachings of the cited prior art to arrive at the specific panel of five genes recited in the claimed methods. In making the rejection, the Office states at pages 12-13 of the Office Action:It would have been obvious to one with ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to include Almog's and Garrido- Gomez's MUCI and APOD in the gene panel disclosed by Diaz-Gimeno because the additional genes provide valuable information and provide for a more reproducible and accurate determination of endometrial status. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to do so because better data would lead to better success in embryo implantation in a human subject. [Emphasis added] Applicant submits that the claimed methods are not obvious in view of the cited prior art references because none of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez (considered alone or in any combination) teach or suggest a method of predicting endometrial receptivity status for embryonic implantation in a human subject that includes, inter alia, determining a gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising Arginase 2 (ARG2), Glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3), Mucin 1 (MUC1), Apolipoprotein D (APOD) and Secretoglobin family 2A member 2 (SCGB2A2) using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction analysis.Applicant submits that, in view of the combined disclosures of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez, one skilled in the art would not have reasonably expected that the claimed method would be able to successfully identifying a human subject as having one of four endometrial statuses (i.e., a receptive endometrial status, non-receptive endometrial status, pre- receptive endometrial status, and post-receptive endometrial status) by determining and comparing the gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising ARG2, GPX3, MUC1, APOD, and SCGB2A2, as none of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez provide any data that would have led one skilled in the art to reasonably expect that a gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising ARG2, GPX3, MUC1, APOD, and SCGB2A2 can be used to successfully identify a human subject as having one of four endometrial statuses.Diaz-Gimeno I discloses "a genomic diagnostic tool for human endometrial receptivity based on the transcriptomic signature" (see Title of Diaz-Gimeno I). Specifically, Diaz-Gimeno I discloses an endometrial receptivity array (ERA) that includes 238 genes and provides a transcriptomic signature defined by 134 genes (see Abstract of Diaz-Gimeno I). According to Diaz-Gimeno I, the ERA is a "bioinformatic test with predictive power to classify the human endometrium gene expression profile that is compatible with LH+7 and to detect the endometrial disorders relating to it" (page 55, left column, last sentence of the first paragraph of Diaz- Gimeno I). Diaz-Gimeno I trained the ERA using samples "obtained from fertile women during their menstrual cycle, and were classified as receptive (R), prereceptive (PR), or proliferative (P)" (page 55, right column, third paragraph, first sentence of Diaz-Gimeno I). Samples in the R group were taken on LH+7 (i.e., days 20-21 of the menstrual cycle); samples in the PR group were collected on days LH+1 to LH+5 of the menstrual cycle (i.e., days 14/15 to 18/19 of the menstrual cycle); and samples in the P group were collected on days 8-12 of the menstrual cycle (see page 55, right column, third paragraph, second sentence of Diaz-Gimeno I).In contrast to the claimed method, the ERA of Diaz-Gimeno I does not teach or suggest identifying a human subject as having a receptive endometrial status, a non-receptive endometrial status, a pre-receptive endometrial status, or a post-receptive endometrial status, where a "post-receptive endometrial status" is defined as an endometrial status that is observed in the days following the window of implantation during the secretory phase of a menstrual cycle (i.e., days 21 to 28 of the menstrual cycle) using the claimed panel of genes. Diaz-Gimeno I does not suggest the presently claimed method which requires identifying a human subject as having one of four endometrial statuses.Of the 134 genes that belong to the endometrial receptivity transcriptomic signature listed in Table 1, Diaz-Gimeno I lists GPX3, which provides a 35.49-fold change, SCGB2A2, which provides a 7.43-fold change, and ARG2, which provides a 4.35-fold change. GPX3 is the only gene of these three that was validated by RT-PCR (see "a" in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I).Nothing in Diaz-Gimeno I provides any specific hint that a panel of genes comprising at least these three genes, GPX3, SCGB2A2, and ARG2 is desirable. While GPX3 is listed in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I as the gene with the highest fold change, both ARG2 and SCGB2A2 are not ranked in the top 10 genes with the highest fold change, nor the top 60 genes with the highest fold change. (SCGB2A2 is ranked 18th and ARG2 is ranked 62nd in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I.) Based on the reading of Diaz-Gimeno I, one skilled in the art would not have been motivated to determine a gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising GPX3, ARG2, and SCGB2A2 as opposed to any of the thousands of possible combinations of five genes listed in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I. There are 34,220 different combinations of three genes that one skilled in the art could have selected from the top 60 genes in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I [60!/(3!(60-3)!))= 34,220]. The Office has provided no hint of what disclosure in Diaz-Gimeno I might motivate one of ordinary skill in the art to select the particular combination of GPX3, ARG2, and SCGB2A2 out of the 34,220 possible three-ERA gene combinations, much less a motivation to include two additional genes not disclosed within the 238 ERA genes, nor do the combined disclosures provide an expectation of success that a panel of genes including GPX3, ARG2, SCGB2A2, APOD and MUC1 would be successful to identify a human subject as having one of four endometrial statuses. In view thereof, one skilled in the art would simply not have been motivated to identify and select GPX3, ARG2, and SCGB2A2 as a starting point for a panel of genes other than impermissible hindsight reconstruction to piece together the claimed invention from the cited art.In an attempt to make up for the deficiencies of Diaz-Gimeno I, the Office cites Almog for allegedly disclosing that "certain genes show upregulation in endometrial biopsies, with two of the genes being apolipoprotein D (APOD) and mucin 1 transmembrane (MUC1)" (Office Action page 12). Almog provides a review of "the association between endometrial injury and implantation" (Abstract of Almog). In particular, Almog discloses the results of a previous study in which the global gene expression of day 21 endometrial samples of patients that had two endometrial biopsies taken in a prior menstrual cycle were compared to day 21 endometrial samples of patients from the control group that did not have any endometrial biopsies (page 2028, left column, "Basic Science Support" of Almog). Analysis of this global gene expression of day 21 endometrial samples of biopsy-treated patients showed 183 upregulated genes and 39 downregulated genes. MUC1, APOD, phospholipase A2 (PLA2) and uroplakin lb (UPIb) were the most upregulated genes (page 2028, left column, "Basic Science Support" of Almog). Like Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog does not teach or suggest identifying a human subject as having one of four endometrial statuses. Instead, Almog focuses on a single day in the menstrual cycle (i.e., day 21 of the menstrual cycle) and a global gene expression profile determined on this single day. Almog also does not teach or suggest predicting endometrial receptivity status for embryonic implantation as Almog concludes that "evidence to date suggests that local endometrial injury might improve the pregnancy rate" (page 2028, right column, last paragraph, first sentence of Almog). According to the disclosure of Almog, the mere act of causing local endometrial injury through an endometrial biopsy taken at any time during the menstrual cycle leads to an improved pregnancy rate. In view of the disclosure of Almog, one skilled in the art would be led to believe that identifying the endometrial status of a human subject is entirely unnecessary as the endometrial biopsy itself improves embryonic implantation. Therefore, Almog teaches away from the claimed method.While Almog discloses that MUC1 and APOD are among the most upregulated 183 genes from the global gene expression profile of day 21 endometrial samples of biopsy-treated patients, nothing in Almog suggests that looking at upregulated genes as opposed to downregulated genes is more informative. Almog also fails to provide any motivation to the skilled person to select the combination of MUC1 and APOD as preferable to any other possible combination of genes. Almog does not even provide a brief overview of the known role of APOD, whereas Almog provides such information for both PLA2 and MUC1. Therefore, upon reading the disclosure of Almog, the skilled artisan would have been motivated, at best, to further investigate PLA2 and MUC1.Even ifpro arguendo, GPX3, ARG2 and SCGB2A2 were selected by the skilled person, other than improper hindsight reconstruction, the combined teachings of Diaz-Gimeno I and Almog provide no reason to add either MUC1 or APOD to a panel of genes from other genes know in the art (e.g., any of the other 181 most upregulated genes from the global gene expression profile and/or 39 downregulated genes of Almog), or to add the specific combination of MUC1 and APOD to the panel of genes.Lastly, Almog states that "many unanswered questions [remain] regarding patient selection, timing, technique, and number of biopsies needed" (page 2028, right column, last sentence of Almog). Therefore, Almog does not provide the necessary guidance or teaching that would have led one skilled in the art to a reasonable expectation of success. Taken together, Almog fails to cure the deficiencies of the primary reference, Diaz-Gimeno I.Garrido-Gomez discloses "profiling the gene signature of endometrial receptivity:clinical results" (Title of Garrido-Gomez). Applicant notes that the ERA of Garrido-Gomez is the same as the ERA of Diaz-Gimeno I. Therefore, the same cohort of genes used in Diaz- Gimeno I is also used in Garrido-Gomez. According to Garrido-Gomez, "the ERA is more accurate than histologic dating and is a highly reproducible method for endometrial dating and diagnosis of endometrial receptivity status" (page 1082, right column, last paragraph, first sentence of Garrido-Gomez). Fig. 1 of Garrido-Gomez provides heatmaps showing ERA gene expression profiles in different endometrial cycle stages (proliferative, pre-receptive, receptive, and post-receptive) and lists the major biological functions regulated in each of these phases.However, as noted above, the ERA does not include determining a gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising ARG2, GPX3, MUC1, APOD, and SCGB2A2. Nothing in the combined disclosures of Garrido-Gomez and Diaz-Gimeno I teach or suggest determining a gene expression profile of a panel of genes that includes this specific panel of five genes or the combination of GPX3, ARG2, and SCGB2A2 specifically. Nothing in Garrido-Gomez provides any specific hint that a panel of genes comprising at least these three genes, GPX3, SCGB2A2, and ARG2 is desirable. According to Garrido-Gomez, MUC1 is provided as an example of a molecule found in the human endometrium, alongside with integrins, calcitonin, leukemia inhibitory factor, cyclo-oxygenase, and homeobox A 10 (page 1079, left column, second paragraph, second sentence of Garrido-Gomez). Garrido-Gomez goes on to say that "despite many of them being phenotypically implicated in murine models, none of them has been translated into clinical practice as an endometrial marker" (page 1079, left column, second paragraph, last sentence of Garrido-Gomez). Therefore, one skilled in the art would not have been motivated to consider including MUC1 in the panel of genes tested in the ERA or to replace MUC1 with another gene in the ERA as MUC1 had not been translated into clinical practice as an endometrial marker at the time of filing.For at least the reasons above, the obviousness rejection of independent claim 30 and its dependent claims (claims 32-36, 38-46, and 49-52) over Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido- Gomez should be reconsidered and withdrawn.2. Claims 31 and 37 are rejected for allegedly being obvious over Diaz-Gimeno I in view of Almog and Garrido-Gomez, and further in view of Diaz-Gimeno (Fertility and Sterility 99(2):508-517 (2013); hereinafter "Diaz-Gimeno II"). Claim 31 depends from claim 30 and includes all of the elements of claim 30. Claim 37 depends from claim 35, which in turn depends from claim 30 and includes all of the elements of claim 30. As stated previously, the combination of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez does not teach or suggest all of the limitations of claim 30, much less the combination of elements in claims 31 and 37.First, like Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez, Diaz-Gimeno II fails to teach or suggest a method of predicting endometrial receptivity status for embryonic implantation that includes, inter alia, determining a gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising ARG2, GPX3, MUC1, APOD, and SCGB2A2. Diaz-Gimeno II discloses "the accuracy and reproducibility of the endometrial receptivity array is superior to histology as a diagnostic method for endometrial receptivity" (Title of Diaz-Gimeno II). The ERA of Diaz-Gimeno II is the same ERA as disclosed in Garrido-Gomez, and includes the same cohort of genes as Diaz- Gimeno I and Garrido-Gomez. Therefore, nothing in the combined disclosures of Diaz-Gimeno I, Garrido-Gomez and Diaz-Gimeno II teach or suggest determining a gene expression profile of a panel of genes that includes this specific panel of five genes or the combination of GPX3, ARG2, and SCGB2A2 specifically. Nothing in Diaz-Gimeno II provides any specific hint that a panel of genes comprising at least GPX3, SCGB2A2, and ARG2 is desirable. As noted above, GPX3 is listed in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I as the gene with the highest fold change, while both ARG2 and SCGB2A2 are not ranked in the top 60 genes with the highest fold change. There are 34,220 different combinations of three genes that one skilled in the art could have selected from the top 60 genes in Table 1 of Diaz-Gimeno I instead of GPX3, ARG2, SCGB2A2 [60!/(3!(60- 3)!))= 34,220]. The Office has provided no hint of what disclosure in the combination of references might motivate one of ordinary skill in the art to select the particular combination of GPX3, ARG2, and SCGB2A2 out of the 34,220 possible three-ERA gene combinations, much less to include two additional genes not disclosed within the 238 ERA genes. This deficiency alone requires withdrawal of the rejection.Second, Diaz-Gimeno II provides no reasonable expectation of success that a panel of genes including GPX3, ARG2, SCGB2A2, APOD and MUC1 would be successful in predicting endometrial receptivity status for embryonic implantation. Therefore, Diaz-Gimeno II does not cure the deficiency of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez.Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the obviousness rejection of claims 31 and 37 be reconsidered and withdrawn.3. Claims 47 and 48 are rejected for allegedly being obvious over Diaz-Gimeno I in view of Almog and Garrido-Gomez, and further in view of Tabibzadeh et al. (Human Reproduction 7(9):1214-1221 (1992); hereinafter "Tabibzadeh"). Claims 47 and 48 depend from claim 30 and includes all of the elements of claim 30. As stated previously, the combination of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez does not teach or suggest all of the limitations of claim 30, much less the combination of elements in claims 47 and 48.Like Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog, and Garrido-Gomez, Tabibzadeh fails to teach or suggest a method of predicting endometrial receptivity status for embryonic implantation that includes, inter alia, determining a gene expression profile of a panel of genes comprising ARG2, GPX3, MUC1, APOD, and SCGB2A2. Tabibzadeh is cited for allegedly disclosing that "endometrial functions can be regulated by cytokines," "the presence of mRNA of the cytokines is found during the entire menstrual cycle, as determined by RT-PCR," and "the reaction volume for the RT-PCR reaction is 17.5 ul" (Office Action page 15). Therefore, Tabibzadeh fails to cure the deficiencies of Diaz-Gimeno I, Almog and Garrido-Gomez.For at least this reason, Applicant respectfully requests that the obviousness rejection of claims 47 and 48 be reconsidered and withdrawn.Double Patenting Claims 30-52 are rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as allegedly being unpatentable over claims 1-23 of U.S. Patent No. 10,918,327.Applicant respectfully requests that the double patenting rejections as applied to claims 30-52 be held in abeyance until otherwise allowable subject-matter has been indicated by the Office.CONCLUSIONApplicant submits that the pending claims are in condition for allowance and such action is hereby respectfully requested. If there are any remaining issues or concerns, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner contact the undersigned at 212-641-2216.The fees for the 1-month extension of time are being paid with this reply on the electronic filing system. Please apply those fees and any other necessary charges or credits to Deposit Account No. 06-1050, referencing Attorney Docket Number 19671-0349002.Respectfully submitted, Date: March 27, 2025 /Jasmine De Cock, Reg.
